lines: West again when the grass says so. A drover who stops is just a man standing in a field, but I'm learning.
My niece wants to take our fleece down to your town. She has a loom and a great many opinions.
The old ram's down? Then we're whole. Go and tell Iona at the gap. She won't leave it to come and find you.
The old ram's still up on the Heather spur, the one with the horns like a pair of handlebars.
Bring him down and we're whole. Iona's at the gap. She's been watching that road for me since the storm.
Old Fang's lying quiet in the barrow? And the well's got its bucket back? Then the moor's ours again.
Only the old ram's still out. Free him and I can take the road west.
Old Fang. Biggest wolf on the moor. He used to follow the flock at a polite distance. Now he's not polite.
Forty-two. Forty-two, all counted. You're a good drover, for someone with no crook.
But the drove well's rope is cut through and the bucket's gone. Something dragged it off toward the barrow.
Take a look at the well. Whatever's in that barrow, it's where the light came down.
The flock's in the thicket by the gap. Shardstruck, all of them. Go gently. They're my sheep.
The night of the starfall the whole flock went wild and ran into the thicket by the gap.
I can't take the road west without them. Free them for me? I'll owe you a fleece.
He's asleep in front of the hut with his paws in the air. Best dog on the moor, again.
Tell me straight. Is he all right?
He runs the road above the gap, up and back. He doesn't know me. Bring him back to himself.
My dog went with the light the night of the storm. He's up on the road, running and running.
Point me at the next storm. I've had my fill of this one.
The ram's down? Then the drover's whole, and I'm a lancer with no road to watch.
I came down off the tops when the sky cracked and held the gap so nothing went for the valley.
If you're going after the rest of that light, you'll want someone who can hold a line. Let me come.
I'm holding the gap. You free the flock. Then we both get to sit down.
Iona. I mind this gap. Sheep, wolves and weather all get asked their business.
The bucket's back on a new rope. The water tastes of peat and stone.
The rope's been bitten through. Paw prints, big ones, lead off across the heather toward the Fold spur's barrow.
An old stone well where the drove road stops to drink.
The hearth is cold and dark. The shard is home.
The hearth is cold and dark where the shard lay.
The great shard sits in the barrow's old hearth like a coal. The well's bucket lies beside it, chewed.
Stars falling, wolves howling, folk running about with lanterns. Busiest week I've had in forty years.
